y1: Jesus was transformed: His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as light. Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets) appeared and talked with Jesus. This illustrates that the entire Old Testament points to Jesus.
y2: Peter wanted to build three tents. At that moment, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice said: 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!' One phrase was added to the voice from His baptism in 3:17: 'Listen.'
y3: 'After six days,' 'a high mountain,' 'a shining face,' 'a cloud,' and 'a voice' all recall the story of Moses in Exodus 24 and 34. Moses reflected God's glory, but Jesus is that glory Himself.
y5: The disciples were afraid and fell to the ground. Jesus came, touched them, and said, 'Get up, and don't be afraid.' When they looked up, they 'saw no one except Jesus.' Both Moses and Elijah disappeared, and only Jesus remained.
y6: On the way down, the disciples asked about the prophecy that Elijah must come first. Jesus says that John the Baptist was that Elijah, and just as people did not recognize him, the Son of Man will also suffer.
y7: Speaking only of glory before the resurrection would cause misunderstanding. People wanted a glorious Messiah without the cross. The glory on the mountain can only be fully understood by passing through the cross.
y8: Failure at the Bottom of the Mountain
y9: At the bottom of the mountain, there was a boy suffering from seizures and disciples who could not heal him. Even though they had received authority in 10:1, they failed. Jesus said, 'Faithless and perverse generation,' and healed the boy.
y10: When the disciples asked why, He said, 'Because of your little faith,' and added, 'If you have faith as small as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, "Move from here to there," and it will move.' The issue is not the size of the faith, but who the faith is directed toward.
y11: 'Little faith' (oligopistia) is a wavering faith mixed with doubt. But 'mustard seed faith,' even if small, is alive and relies completely on God. Just as there is life in a small seed, it is enough for faith to be genuine, even if it is small.
y13: Jesus predicts His death and resurrection for the second time. The disciples were 'deeply grieved.' Then comes the story of the temple tax. Jewish men over twenty paid a half-shekel (two drachmas) temple tax every year.
y14: Jesus says, 'The sons of the king do not pay taxes.' The Son of God, who is the Lord of the temple, does not need to pay. Yet, 'so as not to cause them to stumble,' He tells Peter to pay it and has him find a shekel in a fish's mouth. He chose love over His rights.
y15: Even if you have freedom, giving up that freedom so as not to cause others to stumble is the way of Jesus. Paul also speaks of the same principle (1 Cor. 8:13; Rom. 14:21).
verse: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.'”
prayer: Dear God, thank You for showing that Jesus is Your beloved Son and the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets. Amidst many voices, let me listen to the words of Jesus. Whether on the mountain or at the bottom of the mountain, let me look only to Jesus and live with a living faith like a mustard seed. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: transform. This is the root of the word 'metamorphosis'. The outward appearance did not just change; the hidden glory of God was revealed. The same verb is used in Romans 12:2, 'be transformed by the renewing of your mind.'
d1: touch. It is the same verb used when healing the leper (8:3), the feverish woman (8:15), and the blind men (9:29). Even in a moment of glory, Jesus first touches those who are afraid.
d2: mustard seed. It is connected to the parable of the mustard seed in 13:31. Both the Kingdom of God and faith start small. There is a similar saying in Luke 17:6.
d3: temple tax. It was a tax based on Exodus 30:13, about two days' wages. The one shekel (stater) that came out of the fish was enough for two people. The 'St. Peter's fish' (tilapia) of the Sea of Galilee is still famous today.
